attribution.author: Steve Oak
attribution.subject: Steve Oak / Okkar Kyaw
attribution.role: Product-side full-stack owner / AI product engineer

qualifiers: EcoSmartLoop is a team-built prototype case study; its source does not claim production adoption or measured behavior-change impact.

passages.text: You are holding a greasy takeout container, and all three bins look partly right.
That became the product brief.

UNEP’s 2024 outlook (https://www.unep.org/resources/global-waste-management-outlook-2024) says annual global waste costs could reach USD 640.3B by 2050 without urgent action. In California, one SB 1383 cost scenario models 450,000 businesses with at least five employees (https://www2.calrecycle.ca.gov/Docs/Web/115980). Those numbers explain the scale of the problem. They do not describe EcoSmartLoop adoption, savings, compliance, or impact.

Because we built it at SFBU in Fremont, the California context felt close. SB 1383 (https://calrecycle.ca.gov/organics/slcp/) turned waste sorting into real work for campuses, offices, restaurants, and city-scale programs around the Bay Area. Still, all of that work can come down to one person holding one confusing item.

Maybe it is a pizza box. Maybe it is a coffee cup lid, a takeout container, or a compostable-looking cup that is only compostable somewhere else. The bins are right there: recycling, compost, landfill. Someone may be waiting behind you. You pick the bin that feels least wrong.
The dashboard can come later. The report can come later. First, the person at the bin needs enough confidence to act and move on.

I built the product around that hesitation. The user should not have to become a waste-policy expert to throw something away correctly. The app should bring the decision support to the moment, explain why the recommendation makes sense, and make the next decision feel less random.
The product starts at the bin: a few seconds where signage, memory, and social pressure are not enough.
The bet
A scan was only the first move. EcoSmartLoop had to explain the answer, save it, and make the next decision less of a guess for the person at the bin and the organization reviewing the program later.

The scanner gave us a door into the problem. It did not create trust on its own. A label like “recycle” or “compost” helps only if the person believes it, understands it, and has a way to learn from it later.
The AI agents part only mattered if it helped after the label. Orbi had to explain the answer, cite the reason, remember the decision, and help the user do the next thing.
I kept testing the capstone against four questions.

Would someone actually use it while standing at a bin? Could Orbi feel like an assistant inside the product instead of a green-themed chatbot? Could the whole thing work on a phone without turning into a separate native-app project? And would a business or institution care after the demo was over?

Those questions kept pulling me back from the easy version. A scanner that says “recycle” or “compost” is a good demo. The product I wanted had to explain, remember, teach, and show where the same confusion kept coming back.

Outcome status table Area | Status | Detail | 
 Engagement | User test | Would a normal person use it while standing at a bin? | 
 Orbi | Assistant test | Could guidance feel like part of the product instead of a themed chatbot? | 
 Mobile access | Engineering test | Could the bin-side flow work on a phone without a separate native-app project? | 
 Organization fit | Market test | Could the scanner matter to a campus, office, or food-service team after the demo? |
I used those questions as a filter. If a feature did not make the answer faster, the reasoning clearer, the phone moment easier, or the organization view better, it probably did not belong.
From there, the work moved beyond image classification: cited guidance, rewards, history, quizzes, leaderboards, analytics, and admin surfaces.

EcoSmartLoop did not start as a polished idea. We were kicking around capstone directions, including a multicultural-event scheduling app, before Glenn brought up waste sorting. The room changed a little when we talked about it. It was physical, confusing, local to California, and deep enough for both AI work and product judgment.

The team split became clear by doing the work. Frank Baah and Glenn Marvin Musoke primarily pushed LEAF Engine training and serving. Neelofar helped on frontend and analytics. I took the app around the classifier: scanner, API integration, Orbi AI, rewards, analytics, admin views, responsive UI, and the mobile shell.
After the capstone project event with Glenn, Frank, and me, once the EcoSmartLoop work was already behind us.
Another post-capstone event photo with Neelofar, Frank, and me, after the frontend, analytics, AI, and product pieces had come together.

These were taken after the capstone project event, not during the messy middle of the build. By then, the split was easier to see: Frank and Glenn had pushed the model work, Neelofar had helped the frontend and analytics come together, and I had spent most of my energy making sure the classifier became something a person could actually use.
The classifier could return an answer. My work was making that answer usable through scanner UX, Orbi guidance, rewards, analytics, and a mobile flow.

I was usually worrying about what happened after the model response hit the app: scanner UX, Orbi, product APIs, mobile shell, rewards, and admin analytics.

passages.text: The institution angle came later. At a career fair on top of the LinkedIn (https://www.linkedin.com/) building, I kept hearing a version of the same problem from people around larger teams and startups. Institutions already had waste analytics, diversion reports, and sustainability dashboards. The weak spot was earlier than the report. Most tools helped teams see what happened after the behavior. I kept thinking about the person holding the confusing item before the wrong bin, and the organization that would later have to explain the pattern.
headingPath: My lane was the product around the model

passages.text: The B2B angle came from a simple gap: institutions could report on waste, but the person at the bin still needed help before the mistake.
headingPath: My lane was the product around the model

passages.text: EcoSmartLoop started to look useful for institutions too. The scan still helped the individual first. But if enough people changed the decision at the bin, the organization got better data afterward: cleaner reporting, clearer training gaps, more visible participation, and a better story to tell in sustainability updates. The behavior change work was practical: do more than push the sustainability message. Help the person practice better sorting, reward the right behavior, and give the organization a reason to improve the program.
headingPath: My lane was the product around the model

passages.text: EcoSmartLoop came out of my SFBU M.S. capstone in Fremont, and CalRecycle (https://calrecycle.ca.gov/organics/slcp/) gave the idea a real California operating context. SB 1383 (https://calrecycle.ca.gov/organics/slcp/collection/) means businesses and institutions have to think about education, container access, inspection, recordkeeping, and what happens when organic-waste containers are contaminated.
headingPath: Why a California waste-sorting prototype was worth building

passages.text: In practice, the problem was bigger than a recycling lookup. In an office, campus, or food-service environment, one wrong guess can become repeated behavior: confusing signage, contaminated bins, weak training, and no feedback after the decision. CalRecycle contamination monitoring (https://calrecycle.ca.gov/organics/slcp/collection/contamination/) made that obvious to me. The hard part was not only knowing the class. It was helping people learn around the bin.
headingPath: Why a California waste-sorting prototype was worth building

passages.text: A CalRecycle SB 1383 cost scenario uses 450,000 California businesses with at least five employees (https://www2.calrecycle.ca.gov/Docs/Web/115980). The number stuck with me because it made the project feel large without pretending we had adoption. Nearly half a million businesses in one state is a reminder that waste sorting is a repeated workplace workflow, not a once-a-year climate pledge.
headingPath: Why a California waste-sorting prototype was worth building

passages.text: I also did not want the product to guilt people into caring more. People already try. The better green mission is more practical: make the right action easier and give people a reason to repeat it. The person gets a clearer answer at the bin. The product rewards better sorting. The organization sees what keeps going wrong. The admin has a reason to teach, incentivize, adjust the program, and keep better records for reporting later.
headingPath: Why a California waste-sorting prototype was worth building

passages.text: That mattered because the organization benefit is not only “make a prettier dashboard.” CalRecycle has separate recordkeeping guidance (https://www.calrecycle.ca.gov/organics/slcp/recordkeeping) for SB 1383, and California’s Cool California business guidance (https://coolcalifornia.arb.ca.gov/sustainability-improves-business-profitability) frames sustainability as part of long-term resilience, efficiency, and public accountability. I read those as a startup clue: if the product can improve behavior before the mistake, the organization has cleaner records, better training evidence, and a stronger story after the scan.
headingPath: Why a California waste-sorting prototype was worth building

passages.text: SB 1383 gave the prototype a concrete operating context: education, collection, inspection, and contamination monitoring.
headingPath: Why a California waste-sorting prototype was worth building

passages.text: The policy context shaped the language of the app. I did not want EcoSmartLoop to sound like a rulebook. It needed to answer the question someone has while holding the item: what is this, why does it go there, and what should I do next?
headingPath: Why a California waste-sorting prototype was worth building

passages.text: California organics rules created education, inspection, and contamination-monitoring work before our prototype existed. Feedback around the bin was worth designing because the work already existed for real organizations.
headingPath: Why a California waste-sorting prototype was worth building
The operating pressure was real before the prototype existed

passages.text: The global waste numbers made the stakes feel worth taking seriously, but I try to keep them in the background. UNEP also summarized the report with a sharper public line: the world has to move beyond the “waste era” (https://www.unep.org/news-and-stories/press-release/world-must-move-beyond-waste-era-and-turn-rubbish-resource-un-report). For this project, the big idea was simple: a huge waste problem still shows up as small repeated decisions.
headingPath: Why a California waste-sorting prototype was worth building
The operating pressure was real before the prototype existed

passages.text: There was a real reason to use AI here too. The EPA has funded point-of-disposal AI sorting work (https://cfpub.epa.gov/ncer_abstracts/index.cfm/fuseaction/display.abstractDetail/abstract_id/11235/report/0), and NIST has written about AI and machine learning (https://www.nist.gov/blogs/taking-measure/trash-cash-how-ai-and-machine-learning-can-help-make-recycling-less-expensive) as a way to make recycling more efficient and less expensive for local governments. EcoSmartLoop was a student prototype, but it was aimed at a real physical workflow.
headingPath: Why a California waste-sorting prototype was worth building
The operating pressure was real before the prototype existed

passages.text: Once the team split was clear, my work became easier to describe. I was taking LEAF Engine out of the model notebook and putting it into a product someone could use while holding trash: capture the image, call the classifier safely, show the answer, handle weak confidence, save the scan, and connect the result to Orbi, rewards, history, and organization analytics.
headingPath: What I had to make work

passages.text: Most of the judgment lived in the in-between states. A classifier can say “recycle.” The app still has to answer the real user questions: how sure are we, why should I trust this, what if the answer is uncertain, and what changes after I scan?
headingPath: What I had to make work

passages.text: I did not want the app to stop at “take a picture, get a bin.” That helps once. A real product needed memory.

The sequence became: scan, classify, explain, record, reward, learn, and make the next decision better. The AI agents part was Orbi. It could use sources and app context, make database-backed tool calls, generate UI, trigger app actions, expose uncertainty, and help the user complete the next step.
The diagram shows what happened after classification: explanation, memory, rewards, and the next scan.
After that, EcoSmartLoop stopped feeling like a scanner with a model attached. The scan result now had a place to go: explanation, history, incentives, and organization analytics.
The architecture had to stay readable too. The user-facing app, classifier service, AI assistant, data layer, and organization views could not blur into one mystery box.
EcoSmartLoop had two AI pieces, and I wanted the split to be obvious:
The simplest version: LEAF Engine decided what the item appeared to be, and Orbi helped the person understand what to do with that answer.

LEAF Engine did the photo read. It looked at the uploaded waste image and returned one of four outcomes: compost, recycle, landfill, or unknown, plus confidence/probability output. The shareable model story is simple: four classes, 8K+ image training context, MobileNetV2 transfer learning, 224x224 image input, FastAPI (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/) serving, prediction logging, and a low-confidence path.
Orbi AI handled what happened after the label. I built it with Vercel AI SDK (https://sdk.vercel.ai/) so the assistant could stay model-swappable instead of locked to one provider. Orbi could search and cite sources, call database-backed app tools, render structured UI, generate quiz/reward actions, and take product actions without making the user dig through a dashboard.

Today I would call Orbi the agent part of the product, but I do not mean that in a sci-fi way. It used context, sources, tool calls, generated UI, and product actions to move a user from “I think this is compost” to “here is the recommendation, here is why, here is what changed, and here is what to do next.”

I started from Vercel AI SDK v5 (https://sdk.vercel.ai/) and Vercel AI Elements because the app needed more than a text box: streaming answers, source chips, visible tool progress, quiz actions, reward-aware responses, and app context. A generic prompt would have been faster. It also would have missed the whole reason Orbi existed: knowing where the user was in the product and what action could happen next.
The architecture kept the scanner, classifier, Orbi, memory, rewards, analytics, and admin workflows understandable.

Keeping those jobs separate made the product easier to debug and explain. LEAF Engine handled image classification. Orbi handled explanation and product actions. The app stitched both into scanner, history, rewards, analytics, and admin workflows.
Orbi was where the answer had to earn trust: sources, tool progress, app context, and a next action in the same place.

The Orbi UI came after studying how Perplexity (https://www.perplexity.ai/) makes sources visible and how ChatGPT (https://chatgpt.com/) exposes tool calls, generated UI, and agentic behavior. I wanted the waste answer to show its work: what the model thinks, what source the app used, how uncertain the answer is, and what next action the user can take.

V1 had the obvious pieces: scanner, classification result, dashboard, and basic analytics. It worked, but it felt thin. If the product only tells someone the answer once, why would they come back? And if people do not come back, why would an institution care beyond a one-time demo?

V2 is where it stopped feeling like only a camera flow. We integrated gift-card rewards, leaderboard features, quizzes, achievements, scan history, and admin controls. The question changed from “what bin is this?” to “how do we make the better choice worth repeating?”

A slogan can tell people recycling is important. That is not enough when someone is holding a messy container and the line behind them is moving. The product has to guide the person in the moment, give them feedback, make progress visible, and help the organization see where the confusion keeps coming back.

That direction matched what I was reading about pro-environment behavior. A systematic review of behavior-change interventions (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9486705/) points to feedback, goals, and gamified elements like challenges, points, badges, and leaderboards as useful patterns, while also warning that incentives alone are not magic. The Campus Race to Zero Waste behavior guide (https://campusracetozerowaste.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/RM-Behavior-Change-Strategy-Guide-1.pdf) makes a similar practical point for recycling programs: rewards can help people try new behavior, especially when they are tied to performance.

That is the lane V2 moved into. In EcoSmartLoop, the reward was not supposed to be a random prize pasted on top of a green app. The scan created the learning moment. Orbi explained it. The leaderboard made participation visible. Tremendous gave us a gift-card path an admin could configure. We did not prove redemption at scale, but we did build the surfaces a campus or workplace would need to test whether incentives helped people come back and sort more carefully.
The desktop demo shows the V2 shift: scan once, then keep the user moving through Orbi, rewards, leaderboard progress, achievements, and analytics.

A scan result could lead into Orbi guidance. Progress could lead into a quiz. The same activity could later show up in analytics. That was the behavior-change story I wanted: not one perfect answer, but a product that nudges the next answer to be better.
Rewards were the V2 behavior-change bet: connect points, gift-card potential, progress, and repeat sorting instead of leaving the scan as a one-off answer.

Rewards only made sense if they were tied to real product behavior. I did not want points sprinkled on top of sustainability. I wanted repeated scanning, learning, and correction to feel visible enough that a normal person had a reason to try again, and a manager had a reason to care about the pattern.
Achievements turned repeat sorting into visible progress.
The organization view turned individual behavior into reporting context: where people were confused, where participation was happening, and what needed training.
The leaderboard made participation visible, which matters when the goal is repeated behavior instead of a single correct answer.
History made the product remember decisions, so Orbi and the user had context next time.

Those four screens show what happened after the scan: personal progress, organization analytics, leaderboard pressure, and scan history. Alone, each screen is small. Together, they made V2 feel less like “scan and leave” and more like a place where better habits could build up and organizations could see the change.

The incentive bet was practical: turn the whole sorting experience into a learning path. A person scans an item, understands the reason, saves the result, gets nudged through quizzes and rewards, sees progress on the leaderboard, and gives the organization a clearer view of where people need help. That is much closer to behavior change than just pushing the message harder, and it is more useful for institutions because the report is now connected to the behavior happening at the bin.
The admin side made rewards operational: setup, point rules, and Tremendous-backed gift-card redemption.

The admin screen made the behavior-change idea more serious. A consumer app can hard-code a challenge. An institution-facing product needs someone to decide who can participate, which gift-card rewards are available, how points work, what the leaderboard encourages, and which sorting behaviors are actually worth reinforcing. If this became a startup, that admin layer is where I would explore the business upside too: better participation records, stronger sustainability storytelling, public recognition, and possible grants, rebates, or tax-incentive paths where a real deployment actually qualifies.
The scan path had to come back around: capture, classify, explain, reward, save, and make the next decision easier.
After this point in the build, the scanner was no longer carrying the product by itself. The answer had to be clear at the bin, saved for later, and easier to trust next time.
Mobile was non-negotiable because the use case happens in front of a bin. Nobody wants to open a desktop dashboard to classify trash.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: With a short capstone timeline, we chose responsive web plus Capacitor and focused on the iOS shell. That let us reuse the Next.js (https://nextjs.org/) app, auth behavior, API routes, database logic, and UI work. It also exposed the stuff browser demos hide: WebView cache behavior, login-session persistence, responsive edge cases, and real device differences.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: It worked on phones in the end. Getting there was the painful part. If I were building the long-term mobile product, I would rather use React Native (https://reactnative.dev/) or native SDKs than keep paying the WebView debugging tax.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: Capacitor helped us move fast with one codebase, then real-phone behavior exposed the cost.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The debugging changed my opinion of hybrid mobile. It is fast until platform behavior leaks through. For a capstone, the trade was acceptable. For a real product, I would plan the mobile quality path much earlier.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The mobile shell kept the product honest: the decision had to work at the bin, not later from a desktop.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The phone version changed the way I thought about the product. On desktop, I could make a rich dashboard and hide complexity in space. On mobile, the scanner, upload state, confidence feedback, and Orbi answer had to fit into a few quick taps. The pressure helped. It forced the app to respect the real moment: someone standing at a bin, probably not wanting to think about waste policy.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The mobile demo keeps the flow small: scanner, upload, progress states, achievements, and Orbi inside the same shell.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The classifier integration had its own constraint. The web product needed to talk to a classifier service without brittle browser-to-service behavior, so the app used a server-side classifier proxy.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The other big tradeoff was how I worked with AI assistance while the codebase was growing. I started in Cursor (https://www.cursor.com/). At that time, Cursor felt slower to adopt the newer agent-coding habits I wanted: repo-aware work, terminal-native iteration, custom instructions, tool calls, and repeatable context. A lot of developers were recommending Claude Code (https://claude.ai/) because it was moving quickly in that direction, so I switched about a month in.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The switch helped, but it was not magic. Early AI coding felt easy either way. The hard part was building a way of working around the tool: project instructions, source notes, task boundaries, and small checks after each change.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The switch was about workflow: better repo context, terminal-first iteration, and clearer checks around the agent.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: Claude Code gave me a better base, but I still had to make it fit EcoSmartLoop. The real improvement came from the setup around it: clear project context, narrow tasks, failure evidence, and checks after each change.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: Around then, context engineering started feeling more important than prompt tricks. Better wording did not matter as much as better inputs: logs, source notes, design-spec markdown, and small verification loops. Once the agent saw the exact product state, the exact failure, and the exact design target, the work got less random.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The shift was giving the agent precise project context so it had to guess less.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The same discipline shaped the visual work. Backend progress was fast with AI help, but frontend taste was harder. I tried tools like Bolt, Lovable (https://lovable.dev/), Figma MCP (https://www.figma.com/), and v0 (https://v0.dev/). Most could produce working screens. Too often, the screens still felt like the same generic AI app in different colors.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: What finally clicked was Figma Make (https://www.figma.com/). I designed in Figma, used Figma Make’s GitHub connector (https://github.com/) and click inspector to extract component structure, then turned the design into explicit markdown specs for Claude Code (https://claude.ai/). That extra step kept the design reasoning alive instead of handing the agent a screenshot and hoping it guessed the intent.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The design workflow became specific on purpose: Figma structure, inspected components, markdown specs, then Claude Code implementation.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The frontend and design workflow took more steps, but it upgraded the experience for both sides. As a developer, I had clearer intent before asking Claude Code to implement. As a user, the app felt more intentional: scanner feedback, rewards, Orbi, and analytics started to feel like one product instead of the same-looking AI slop with different labels.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: Motion was part of the same push. I bought access to Motion Plus (https://motion.dev/) so I could study how better products use motion for feedback, continuity, and state changes. That showed up in scanner progress, achievement feedback, leaderboard updates, and transitions that made the app feel more intuitive instead of flat.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: Motion was not decoration here. It helped scan results, achievement feedback, and leaderboard updates feel responsive.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The challenge list became clearer as the product got more real. There was no heroic rewrite. There were small, specific improvements: train more, test on real devices, make Orbi use tools, tighten the design, and build the missing AI UI pieces ourselves.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The animation marks the moment the fixes started to feel connected: model consistency, mobile behavior, Orbi specificity, UI polish, and custom AI chat states.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: The lesson was simple enough to reuse later: take a vague product risk, make it concrete, and check whether the fix actually changed the experience.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

Outcome status table Area | Status | Detail | 
 LEAF consistency | Still needed evaluation | Frank and Glenn expanded the 8K+ training context and serving path; exact public accuracy still needs a separate evaluation run. | 
 Mobile cache | Resolved for prototype | Real device testing exposed WebView cache, login-session, and responsive-state issues that browser testing missed. | 
 Generic AI | Improved | Orbi moved toward tools, cited guidance, quiz actions, rewards context, and organization data. | 
 Flat UI | Improved | Figma Make, explicit design specs, and Motion Plus helped the app feel intentionally designed instead of generic. | 
 AI chat UI | Implemented | Vercel AI SDK and AI Elements became the base for streaming, source chips, tool progress, and structured product states. |
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: By the end, the open questions were clearer than they had been at the start. The prototype held together, and the next work was obvious: model evaluation, production mobile reliability, deeper Orbi behavior, and real organization usage.
headingPath: The tradeoffs that made it real

passages.text: I do not want the stack to read like a grocery list. The reason it mattered was movement: the item had to move from camera to classifier to Orbi to history, rewards, and admin review without feeling like five disconnected demos.
The stack connected the scanner, classifier service, Orbi, database, rewards, mobile shell, and motion work.

Next.js (https://nextjs.org/) and TypeScript carried the app people touched. Capacitor put that app into an iOS shell. Supabase, Prisma, and BetterAuth handled identity, scans, rewards, and organization data. AWS, FastAPI, and Python kept the classifier callable. Vercel AI SDK powered Orbi. Tremendous shaped the reward path. Motion helped the product respond instead of sitting there like a static dashboard.

The $640.3B waste-cost projection and the 450K California-business cost scenario explain why I cared about the problem. EcoSmartLoop did not produce those numbers. It was a prototype aimed at one small part of that bigger operating mess: the decision before the item hits the wrong bin.

The prototype was still interesting without pretending it was already deployed. We had a working path from image classification to Orbi guidance, rewards, analytics, mobile shell, and admin views. Missing was the operating evidence a real institution would ask for: production pilots, repeated usage, compliance results, incentive-program fit, and final model-quality reporting.

For LEAF Engine, I can describe the public shape clearly: 8K+ images as training context, four output classes, confidence/probability output, and a serving path the product could call. Before I would make a stronger model-quality claim, I would want the exact split, thresholds, confusion matrix, precision, recall, and failure examples sitting beside it.
LEAF Engine had enough shape to build around: 8K+ image context, four classes, confidence output, and a serving path the product could call.

The next version would need a clean evaluation run, not better screenshots. I would test confusing California waste items across unaided human guesses, LEAF-only output, and LEAF plus Orbi guidance. That benchmark would show whether the product actually beats guesswork.
The product improved as the scan gained context: classify the item, explain the answer, remember the decision, and make the next attempt easier.
The product became more convincing when one answer turned into memory, guidance, rewards, and a better next scan.

At that point, EcoSmartLoop felt bigger than a scanner demo to me. A classifier can answer once. A product can remember the answer, explain it, incentivize better behavior, and show an organization where confusion keeps happening.

Outcome status table Area | Status | Detail | 
 Task | Known | Classify waste images into compost, recycle, landfill, or unknown. | 
 Architecture | Known | MobileNetV2 transfer learning, 224x224 image input, and FastAPI serving. | 
 Dataset | Known | 8K+ labeled images used as classifier training context. | 
 Output | Known | Predicted class, confidence, and probability data returned to the product. | 
 Final metrics | Needs evaluation | Exact accuracy, precision, recall, F1, thresholds, split, and confusion matrix still need a dedicated evaluation run. |

The prototype can honestly say this much: it turned a classifier result into guidance, memory, rewards, and an organization view. Stronger model-quality numbers should come from the next evaluation run.

We treated the capstone like a possible startup for a while. We prepared venture-style pitches, thought through customer segments, and talked seriously about what it would take to move from prototype to institution-ready product.
headingPath: Why we did not turn it into a company yet

passages.text: The capstone poster captures the direction we were pitching by the end: vision, intelligence, growth loop, and architecture.
headingPath: Why we did not turn it into a company yet

passages.text: By the end, the pitch had grown into the whole product arc: computer vision at the bin, Orbi explaining the recommendation, incentives helping people repeat better sorting, and organization tools around the activity.
headingPath: Why we did not turn it into a company yet

passages.text: The pitch flyer is the startup-shaped version of the project before we chose to take the learning into industry first.
headingPath: Why we did not turn it into a company yet

passages.text: Then we made the decision that fit where we actually were: take the learning into industry first.
headingPath: Why we did not turn it into a company yet

passages.text: A serious waste-tech company needs more than a strong capstone. It needs pilots, operations knowledge, procurement cycles, compliance proof, model evaluation, customer support, deployment discipline, and a clear path through institutions. It would also need to prove the business case honestly: better sorting behavior, cleaner reporting, stronger public sustainability stories, and possible incentive, grant, rebate, or tax-credit opportunities where the organization actually qualifies. I would treat those as next-step business research, not as something the capstone already proved. We were early in our careers and wanted more experience before taking on that burden.
headingPath: Why we did not turn it into a company yet

passages.text: That decision belongs in the story. EcoSmartLoop was a serious team-built prototype, and it taught me how to think about AI products, incentives, and evidence. I am glad we treated it with ambition. I am also glad we did not pretend a capstone was already a company.
headingPath: Why we did not turn it into a company yet

passages.text: EcoSmartLoop changed how I think about AI products.

Before this project, I cared mostly about making the AI work. After it, I cared more about the product around the AI: context engineering, tool design, source trust, user feedback, low-confidence handling, analytics, and the interface states that make a model usable.

It changed the way I build too. I started writing better source notes before asking an agent to help. I got stricter about logs, screenshots, design specs, and acceptance checks. I became more interested in the moment between model output and user action than in the model result alone.

I still use that lesson in my current work. After EcoSmartLoop, I built mini AI apps like Craftie and YouSoul faster because the workflow had changed: smaller context packets, better logs, reusable agent skills, clearer design specs, and more aggressive verification. I no longer treat AI as a blank chat box. I ask what context it has, what tools it can use, what it remembers, what needs to be checked, and how the user can see why the answer should be trusted.
The model mattered. Orbi made the answer usable. What I still care about most is the work around the model: make the prediction work, then make the decision clearer, safer, and easier to repeat.

documents.title: LinkedIn Growth Loop: High-Autonomy Agent Teams That Self-Improve

attribution.author: Steve Oak
attribution.subject: Steve Oak / Okkar Kyaw
attribution.role: Agent workflow owner / AI product engineer
qualifiers: The page describes a bounded professional-relationship workflow with operator controls and a feedback loop.

passages.text: I had been using agents for long enough to feel the gap between the demo and the daily reality.
headingPath: Agents Are Overhyped Until They Own The Work

passages.text: Paid tools, other teams’ agents, and agents I built myself could all do impressive one-off tasks. The weak point came after the task finished. I still had to read the logs, inspect the run, patch the prompt, notice the missing report, update the browser step, and decide what should happen tomorrow.
headingPath: Agents Are Overhyped Until They Own The Work

passages.text: That made the word “agent” feel inflated. If I still carried the plan, the memory, the judgment, and the next decision, I was still the operator. The tool had improved the interface, but the work still lived in my head.
headingPath: Agents Are Overhyped Until They Own The Work

passages.text: The industry has been circling the same problem. Anthropic writes about long-running harnesses because agents need state, budgets, continuation, and recovery. Codex /goal (https://github.com/openai/codex/releases/tag/rust-v0.128.0) exists because longer work needs a persistent objective. Ralph-style loops, Paperclip, Karpathy’s autoresearch (https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch), and Arize’s telemetry writing all point in the same direction: once the work lasts longer than one chat, the model becomes only one piece of the job.
headingPath: Agents Are Overhyped Until They Own The Work

passages.text: The idea that really stuck with me came from Factory Missions (https://factory.ai/news/missions). Their framing was simple: stop trying to make one agent do everything. Use an orchestrator, workers, validators, and research agents because each role fails in a different way. That changed how I thought about my own systems. I stopped asking, “Can one agent handle this?” and started asking, “What team would make this work trustworthy?”
headingPath: Agents Are Overhyped Until They Own The Work

passages.text: The gap was around the run: memory, recovery, reports, evaluation, and a trustworthy next decision.
headingPath: Agents Are Overhyped Until They Own The Work

passages.text: THE OPERATING LAYER
headingPath: Agents Are Overhyped Until They Own The Work

passages.text: Trust came from the operating layer around the model: state, reports, validators, research, recovery, and a next decision the system could explain.
headingPath: Agents Are Overhyped Until They Own The Work

passages.text: The need became concrete during a brief HyperSkalers project. One of the projects there was about building relationships through in-house agent teams instead of handing the work to another vendor workflow and hoping it adapted.
headingPath: The In-House Need Made It Serious

passages.text: While working through that, the actual shape of the problem became clearer: find the right people, understand why they fit, keep the outreach relevant, follow the conversation, and avoid turning serious networking into noisy outbound.
headingPath: The In-House Need Made It Serious

passages.text: The obvious tools had tradeoffs. Some were expensive. Some were locked into one platform. Some were slow to adapt when the platform changed. Some created restriction risk because the user had very little control over how the work was being done.
headingPath: The In-House Need Made It Serious

passages.text: The conclusion was clear enough: an in-house agent team would be more interesting than another vendor workflow. It could stay close to the data, explain its own runs, improve from real outcomes, and keep sensitive choices behind approval.
headingPath: The In-House Need Made It Serious

passages.text: That was the point where I started going deeper. The goal was bigger than LinkedIn automation (https://www.linkedin.com/): I wanted to know whether agent teams could run an actual business workflow without me holding every step together.
headingPath: The In-House Need Made It Serious

passages.text: Networking was the useful test surface because it forced the system to care about fit, context, tone, follow-up, and real response signals.
headingPath: The In-House Need Made It Serious

passages.text: LinkedIn Growth Loop became the first project where the idea actually worked for me.
headingPath: LinkedIn Became The First Real Success

passages.text: The visible workflow was relationship work. The deeper project was autonomy: agents choosing targets, preparing context, acting inside limits, reporting what happened, learning from outcomes, and feeding the next pass without me manually operating the whole thing.
headingPath: LinkedIn Became The First Real Success

passages.text: Among the agent projects I had tried, this was my first real success with multiple agents doing the jobs at high autonomy. The autonomy was bounded: routine work moved out of my hands, while override, approval, and rollback stayed available.
headingPath: LinkedIn Became The First Real Success

passages.text: The first real win was the moment the loop finally had real feedback to react to.
headingPath: LinkedIn Became The First Real Success

passages.text: LinkedIn (https://www.linkedin.com/) was useful because the feedback was immediate and hard to fake. Someone connects, ignores, replies, keeps talking, or makes it obvious the note missed. In professional and high-skill relationship work, that is risky. A bad interaction is public enough to care about. But it is also worth it because those real outcomes are what a self-improving system can actually learn from.
headingPath: LinkedIn Became The First Real Success

passages.text: The discovery was almost accidental. Start with one small skill, run it against the real world, evaluate the result, then widen the loop only after the team can explain what happened. Without that feedback, agent work turns into weeks of polishing imaginary behavior.
headingPath: LinkedIn Became The First Real Success

passages.text: The loop started working when each run left more usable context for the next one: reports, approval, memory, browser checks, research, and better rules.
headingPath: LinkedIn Became The First Real Success

passages.text: The work moved out of my head when the next run could start from reports, memory, checks, research, and rules instead of starting from me.
headingPath: LinkedIn Became The First Real Success

passages.text: The first version was intentionally small.

I had a list of people from CRM context and LinkedIn (https://www.linkedin.com/) Navigator-style targeting. The daily job was simple: review the list, understand why each person belonged there, write a personalized connection note, send or skip, then record what happened.

That small loop had the right shape. It had a target, context, an action, a result, and a next decision. It also had real constraints: avoid generic notes, avoid blasting people, stop repeating stale examples, and save model calls for decisions that needed judgment.

Later, the scope widened into target discovery, feed interaction, response tracking, follow-up state, and outcome comparison. Starting small made that expansion possible because the early runs created feedback quickly instead of hiding problems behind a large automation plan.
Target review gave the loop a real starting point: who this person is, why they fit, and whether the next action should happen.
Response tracking made the next run smarter: the system could keep the outcome, compare it with prior choices, and decide what changed.
The first loop had to stay small enough that a weak target, a bland note, a missed follow-up, or a broken browser action would show up immediately.
The first real design decision was to stop treating the workflow as one agent. I split it into two operating groups:

People work handled target lists, scoring, context, connection notes, send-or-skip decisions, and follow-up state.
Public interaction handled relevant posts, cooldown checks, duplicate-risk watching, and response signals.

Around those groups, I needed the same shape I liked from Factory’s mission model: an orchestrator to keep the work moving, workers to own specific jobs, validators to stop unsafe actions, and research agents to keep the environment fresh.
A bad target, a weak note, a browser miss, and a duplicate-risk problem needed separate owners. Filing all of them under “the agent failed” would hide the fix.
The team became easier to trust when execution, research, reports, memory, validation, and override had separate jobs.

Once the roles were separated, the reports got sharper. I could tell whether a miss belonged to targeting, writing, browser control, duplicate prevention, research, or orchestration instead of treating everything as a prompt problem.
OpenClaw (https://openclaw.ai/) was my main worker and orchestrator for this version. It ran the recurring work, coordinated tools, reported status, and kept the lanes moving.

Hermes (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/) was useful in a different role. The overall sentiment around it was that Hermes worked better for self-improvement and memory-oriented work, so I treated it more like an advisor: research what changed, learn from the feedback loop, keep audience and platform signals fresh, and feed better advice back into the next decision.

That pairing was personal preference. I could have forced everything into one harness, but I wanted to see what each one was actually good at, then make them cooperate instead of pretending one tool should own every job.

The broader lesson traveled beyond the specific tools. Today the same operating model could be built with Codex (https://openai.com/codex/), Claude Code (https://www.anthropic.com/claude-code), OpenAI Agents (https://openai.com/), Ralph-style loops, Factory-style missions, or another open-source harness. The team design mattered most: execution, research, memory, reporting, review, validation, and approval each needed a clear job.

That separation made autonomy easier to trust. The research side could advise without silently changing live behavior. The orchestrator had to turn evidence into a proposal, a low-risk change, a skip, or an approval path.
OpenClaw kept the recurring work moving. Hermes stayed closer to research, memory, and improvement advice. The system worked because those jobs were separate.

Modern agent harnesses are moving beyond the terminal because messaging channels already feel natural. Telegram (https://telegram.org/), Slack (https://slack.com/), Discord (https://discord.com/), iMessage (https://www.apple.com/ios/messages/), and similar surfaces are where people already check status and respond quickly. That makes agent work feel less like babysitting a terminal and more like managing a teammate.

OpenClaw (https://openclaw.ai/) and Hermes (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/) already supported messaging channels, including Telegram-style control. The built-in reporting worked, but each channel has different formatting strengths. Plain text was leaving too much value on the table, and over months it drained attention. A report would arrive, but I still had to parse the story: what changed, what failed, whether I needed to care, and where the useful detail lived.

So I built a dedicated Telegram control room and forced the harnesses to report through it. It supported the richer Telegram formats I actually wanted: sections, formatting, controls, compact summaries, and hidden detail. Every message had two versions inside it. The visible layer was human-friendly and ADHD-friendly: status, key metrics, failures, recommendation, and controls. Underneath, the same message carried machine-friendly detail: run IDs, run details, artifact paths, source references, proposed changes, logs, and control actions.
The first view was a report glance: enough status to know whether the run needed attention.
Worker reports used human-friendly formatting first: what happened, what changed, and what I should do next.
The LinkedIn worker reports stayed compact so I could scan target, action, failure, and recommendation without opening logs.
Hermes reported like an advisor: research, risks, and next recommendations instead of pretending to be another executor.
The machine layer lived underneath the human summary: run detail, reusable context, and next-agent handoff data.
Collapsed mode kept the channel readable while preserving the deeper machine-friendly format for follow-up investigation.

That changed the development pace. I could scan the summary during the day, then hand the same message to another agent when something needed deeper investigation. The report stopped being a status ping and became shared working memory.
APIs are more valuable than ever in the agent era. They are still the cleanest path when they expose the work clearly. I kept running into cases where the practical route still lived in the browser.
headingPath: Browser Control Kept The Cost Honest

passages.text: Some workflows live inside the same browser surfaces humans already use. API paths can be limited, expensive, messy, or too narrow for the actual job. In those cases, browser control becomes part of the agent stack.
headingPath: Browser Control Kept The Cost Honest

passages.text: That choice reduced API dependency and created a different kind of work. Browsers change. Platforms change. Labels move. DOM structure shifts. A browser agent has to handle small changes cheaply instead of spending a heavy model call on every tiny step.
headingPath: Browser Control Kept The Cost Honest

passages.text: I made routine actions as programmatic as possible: SOPs, recorder flows, page calibration, cached control knowledge, button and field checks, page-state checks, and bounded recovery before heavier intelligence. Known actions should run cheaply. Changed pages should try narrow recovery before asking a model to reason from scratch.
headingPath: Browser Control Kept The Cost Honest

passages.text: The model still belonged in the judgment-heavy moments: understanding a person’s context, deciding whether a note sounded human, comparing interaction strategies, and summarizing the result. A Gemini Flash-class model (https://gemini.google.com/) was enough for those steps. I saved the heavier models for work that actually needed them.
headingPath: Browser Control Kept The Cost Honest

passages.text: Browser control stayed useful when it was treated as an operating surface: known steps stayed cheap, changed pages had recovery paths, and judgment-heavy moments still went to the model.
headingPath: Browser Control Kept The Cost Honest

passages.text: That pressure is showing up across browser-agent work too. Stagehand action caching (https://www.browserbase.com/stagehand) avoids repeated inference for known actions. Playwright Test Agents (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-agents) separates planner, generator, and healer roles around repeatable browser tasks. If I were rebuilding this now, I would also look hard at browser-use/browser-harness (https://browser-use.com/) because I only found it after the project was already far along, and its open-source browser-harness direction is closer to the self-healing foundation I wish I had started with.
headingPath: Browser Control Kept The Cost Honest

passages.text: The team became more reliable when each run stopped ending as one vague success or failure. I needed to know what kind of failure happened and which agent should learn from it.
The report had to separate quality, safety, cost, outcome, and change decisions so the next agent knew where to improve.
headingPath: What The Report Had To Separate

passages.text: The report shape made the next improvement obvious without exposing individual outcomes or exact run numbers.
headingPath: What The Report Had To Separate

passages.text:
Outcome status table Area | Status | Detail | 
 Target quality | Tracked | Did the person match the audience, source rule, and relationship goal? | 
 Action success | Tracked | Did the intended action complete, skip safely, or fail with a useful reason? | 
 Response signal | Private | Connection, reply, conversation, pending, failed, and follow-up signals stay in private learning history. | 
 Duplicate risk | Guarded | Reliable post identity, seen-state, cooldowns, and learning-history checks protect public interactions. | 
 Browser health | Reported | Selector misses, page drift, timing, browser readiness, and recovery attempts are tracked separately from model judgment. | 
 Run health | Reported | Reports carry status, duration, errors, run details, skipped work, and next-run notes. | 
 Cost behavior | Designed | Programmatic steps stay cheap; model calls are reserved for personalization, summaries, and proposal judgment. | 
 Proposal decision | Approval based | An improvement can apply, wait, skip, need approval, or require a way to undo it. | 
 Intervention count | Summarized | The workflow tracks where Oak still steps in; the public page explains the category without presenting exact reduction numbers. |
headingPath: What The Report Had To Separate

passages.text: The scorecard was necessary because the system mixed deterministic and non-deterministic behavior. A browser miss, a stale target, a weak note, and a risky proposal each needed to teach a different lesson.
headingPath: What The Report Had To Separate

passages.text: At first, the report was for me. It summarized the run, gave research notes, suggested rule changes, and told me where to look next.
headingPath: What The Report Had To Separate

passages.text: The higher-autonomy step came later, when I stopped being the main destination for every suggestion. The report became input for the next group of agents. Research notes, failures, examples, and proposed rules flowed back into the growth loop instead of stopping with me.
headingPath: What The Report Had To Separate

passages.text: After that, improvement became a chain instead of a feeling:
headingPath: What The Report Had To Separate

passages.text:
A run created run details, outcomes, skips, failures, and report rows.
Learning history updated examples, run notes, and strategy memory.
Hermes (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/) added research, memory context, and platform-risk signals.
OpenClaw (https://openclaw.ai/) turned that evidence into a proposed improvement or a bounded change.
The next Telegram report explained what changed, what stayed blocked, and what the following run should use.
headingPath: What The Report Had To Separate

passages.text: The report stopped being the end of the run. It became the handoff that helped the next agent improve the next pass.
headingPath: What The Report Had To Separate

passages.text: The loop became useful when the proposed change stayed readable. The next report had to show why a change was worth making, what would actually change, and where the system should stop or ask before touching live behavior.
headingPath: What The Report Had To Separate

passages.text: Self-improvement became trustworthy when the proposal stayed small: evidence, change, risk, and a clear next action.
headingPath: What The Report Had To Separate

passages.text: Low-risk changes could apply automatically. Weak ideas were skipped. Sensitive changes went through approval because they touched platform behavior, schedules, or public-facing actions. Anything risky needed a way to undo it before it came near the live workflow.
headingPath: What The Report Had To Separate

passages.text: That matched where agent tooling was already heading. OpenAI agent evals (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agent-evals) and Anthropic’s agent eval writing (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents) both push people to inspect trajectories, tool calls, and handoffs alongside final answers. Paperclip (https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip), Ralph Loop (https://blakecrosley.com/blog/ralph-agent-architecture), and Karpathy’s autoresearch (https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch) point toward agents that keep or discard changes based on measured outcomes. Inside this workflow, the same idea became practical when reports became the next run’s working material.
headingPath: What The Report Had To Separate

passages.text: There were plenty of failures over months: stale selectors, noisy targets, weak examples, missing context, skipped reports, and decisions that looked reasonable until real feedback exposed the gap.
headingPath: One Failure That Forced Better Rules

passages.text: One visible failure came from the feed agent sometimes struggling to tell two posts apart. Different posts from the same person could look too similar unless the run proved exactly which post it was touching.
headingPath: One Failure That Forced Better Rules

passages.text: For relationship work, that mistake is visible. A duplicate public interaction makes the system look careless. It also exposed a rule I wanted everywhere: prove the object first, or stop.
headingPath: One Failure That Forced Better Rules

passages.text: The failure turned into a simple rule: prove the object first, or stop before public action.
headingPath: One Failure That Forced Better Rules

passages.text: I moved that risk into rules and run memory. The agent needed fewer chances to be careful and more places where the run would refuse to continue.
headingPath: One Failure That Forced Better Rules

passages.text: After that change, a report could show more than completion. It could show that the risky behavior had a clear stop condition around it. The next version required reliable post identity before action instead of trusting the agent to notice the problem later.
headingPath: One Failure That Forced Better Rules

passages.text: For me, this was the first clear success at building agents that self-automate in a bounded lane without me operating every step.
headingPath: What Moved Out Of My Head

passages.text: The team worked because routine actions, approval paths, recovery, and override were separated instead of all being called autonomy.
headingPath: What Moved Out Of My Head

passages.text: Trust came from the boundary: routine work could move, sensitive changes had to ask, and risky changes needed a way back.
headingPath: What Moved Out Of My Head

passages.text: High-autonomy agents can take over routine work when the surrounding operating layer is strong enough. The model matters, but so do orchestration, worker roles, validators, evaluation, reports, cost controls, browser resilience, approval paths, rollback, and memory.
headingPath: What Moved Out Of My Head

passages.text: LinkedIn Growth Loop (https://www.linkedin.com/) is the relationship-work version of that idea. The same approach applies to serious applied-AI systems: start with one small real skill, launch it, collect real feedback, make the work readable, route reports back into the agent team, and expand autonomy only after the team can explain itself.
headingPath: What Moved Out Of My Head

passages.text: The daily feeling changed. I was no longer waking up to manage every tiny run. I was watching a small team do the work, explain the result, check the environment, and improve the next pass. My job moved from operator to reviewer, and even the review suggestions started becoming inputs for other agents.
headingPath: What Moved Out Of My Head

passages.text: That was the shift: I was no longer pushing every step forward. I was watching the system carry the loop.
headingPath: What Moved Out Of My Head

passages.text: I want to keep building in that direction: high-autonomy harnesses, internal tools, plugins, browser agents, and workflows where orchestrators, workers, validators, research, memory, and reports keep improving each other.
headingPath: What Moved Out Of My Head

passages.text:
The article published 2026-04-20 reports this chart: Where Autonomy Was Allowed.
This is a qualitative operating boundary, not a measured score.
Trust came from the boundary: routine work could move, sensitive changes had to ask, and risky changes needed a way back.
Runs alone: Scheduled runs, local state updates, examples/reflections, research collection, reports, and eligible low-risk changes.
Asks first: Structural changes, sensitive platform behavior, schedule changes, rollback actions, mission dispatches, and risky proposals.
Can recover: A way back: pending action, canary/eval check, pause/resume, and event log.
Oak can stop: Final stop, direction, and approval authority.
headingPath: What Moved Out Of My Head

documents.title: Oakminder: Productivity AI Agent and Distribution Studio

attribution.author: Steve Oak
attribution.subject: Steve Oak / Okkar Kyaw
qualifiers: The case study describes Oakminder as App Store live and its TikTok/UGC studio as internal; usage and performance metrics remain private.

passages.text: I had tried enough productivity tools to know the market was crowded. Reminder apps, calendars, task managers, Kanban boards, habit tools - I have used some version of all of them for decades.
headingPath: Why I Built Another Reminder App

passages.text: The frustrating part was that many of them tried to cover everything, then still fell apart around the small moments that decide whether a reminder actually gets handled. One app can show the notification but make Bulk reminder management painful. Another can support bulk changes but give you weak control over what happens when those reminders interrupt you. Some handle recurring rules but make snoozing feel rigid. Some are good at capture and weak at resolution.
headingPath: Why I Built Another Reminder App

passages.text: Oakminder App Store graphics showing the product story across voice, agenda, progress, snooze, alarms, notification actions, and roadmap.
headingPath: Why I Built Another Reminder App

passages.text: Those gaps get worse when the schedule changes in bulk. A reminder should be the smallest possible interruption, but mine usually felt like a chore: unlock the phone, open the app, find the reminder, reschedule it, and hope the new time sticks. Even with AI moving quickly, reminder follow-through still feels early. The tools have not fully caught up to the real mess of notifications, recurring tasks, bulk changes, and attention switching.
headingPath: Why I Built Another Reminder App

passages.text: That was the loop after years of reminder tools: useful apps, same tiny interruption problem, over and over.
headingPath: Why I Built Another Reminder App

passages.text: Oakminder started from that friction. I wanted a Productivity AI agent that could support the annoying details in one place: snooze from the notification, complete from the notification, bulk-manage reminders when the schedule changes, defer without digging, keep the reminder visible, sync the decision anywhere else I might see it, and integrate AI and agent features where they actually change the reminder state.
headingPath: Why I Built Another Reminder App

passages.text: Foundation MVP
headingPath: Why I Built Another Reminder App

passages.text: The current build is the foundation: cross-platform notification behavior, bulk reminder management, and a voice AI agent that changes real reminder state. It is built to support the nuances that kept breaking my own reminder workflow, and to keep improving for people with the same problem.
headingPath: Why I Built Another Reminder App

passages.text: The internal distribution studio built around Oakminder.
headingPath: Why I Built Another Reminder App

passages.text: The app still starts with the obvious path: create the reminder, see it at the right time, then handle it without rebuilding the whole plan.
headingPath: From Tap Flow To Voice Agent

passages.text: Of course, most people start with taps. That still has to work. But after using enough general AI agents, I kept wanting a simpler product question: what if the reminder app had a Voice agent that could do the real reminder work? Most general agents are too broad for this moment, and most productivity reminder apps still stop before agentic actions get deep. That is the lane I explored and implemented.
headingPath: From Tap Flow To Voice Agent

passages.text: A quick overview demo of Oakminder 1.0.
headingPath: From Tap Flow To Voice Agent

passages.text: Oakminder turns a typed, tapped, or spoken request into a real reminder: title, date, time, category, recurrence, snooze behavior, notification schedule, alarm behavior, Live Activity timing, and account state. When the reminder fires, the next action should stay cheap. Snooze it. Complete it. Defer it. Keep it visible until it is actually handled.
headingPath: From Tap Flow To Voice Agent

passages.text: The app becomes useful when a reminder can move from rough input to structured state, native urgency, action, sync, and visibility.
headingPath: From Tap Flow To Voice Agent

passages.text: This is workflow and feature coverage for reminder follow-through only; it is not retention, habit, performance, or user-outcome data.
headingPath: From Tap Flow To Voice Agent

passages.text: Everything else was there to support that path. The app could have grown into another heavy productivity dashboard. I wanted the opposite: enough structure for durable reminders, a real-time Cross-platform sync foundation for iOS and Android, bulk schedule changes, and meaningful voice-agent actions, with few enough steps that I would still use it when my attention was already split.
headingPath: From Tap Flow To Voice Agent
