passages.text: The main design decision was to treat the notification as part of the reminder workflow, not a delivery detail.
headingPath: Notification Actions Had To Carry More

passages.text: Most reminder apps already support some version of Notification actions. The harder part was making the tap behave like real account state, not a local button on one phone. Oakminder tries to keep the decision where the interruption already happened. If a reminder fires while I am walking, cooking, driving, or in the middle of another task, I should be able to buy the right amount of time without searching through screens.
headingPath: Notification Actions Had To Carry More

passages.text: Custom snooze is the clearest example. The app supports presets, but real life does not always fit five, ten, or fifteen minutes. A meeting might end in 22 minutes. Laundry might need 91. I wanted control without ceremony.
headingPath: Notification Actions Had To Carry More

passages.text: The tap only feels intuitive if the notification, account state, next reminder time, and other devices update together.
headingPath: Notification Actions Had To Carry More

passages.text: That sounds small until the app has to sync it in real time. A snooze tap from a notification is not a button by itself. It changes account-backed reminder state, schedules the next interruption, updates or clears native urgency surfaces, and makes sure other signed-in devices stop showing stale urgency.
headingPath: Notification Actions Had To Carry More

passages.text: Oakminder is iOS-first and App Store live today, but I did not want the product idea to be locked to one platform. The foundation is account-backed so iOS and Android can share the same reminder truth over time, with iPad, macOS, Apple Watch, and web able to follow the same model later. The product model is account-backed first: reminders follow the account, not one device.
headingPath: Notification Actions Had To Carry More

passages.text: Real-time sync across the app and different platforms, covering not only app features but native notification management too.
headingPath: Notification Actions Had To Carry More

passages.text: One of the hardest parts of Oakminder sits behind the simple action.
headingPath: The Architecture Behind A Simple Tap

passages.text: When the user taps snooze, the product has to keep several things honest at once. The phone should feel instant. The backend still has to know exactly what changed.
headingPath: The Architecture Behind A Simple Tap

passages.text: I chose Convex (https://www.convex.dev/) because it made real-time data changes easier to build without spending the whole project buried in infrastructure decisions. In plain English, it is the shared source of truth for reminders, recurrence, completion history, devices, notification scheduling, premium access, and AI credits. The Expo app (https://expo.dev/) owns the live mobile behavior for the iOS-first app and keeps the Android path in the same product model. Clerk (https://clerk.com/) handles identity. RevenueCat (https://www.revenuecat.com/) and Water Drops (the in-app currency name for AI credits) keep subscriptions, consumables, and AI usage tied to the account. Push, APNs/FCM, AlarmKit, Live Activity, and silent cleanup project that state back onto the phone.
headingPath: The Architecture Behind A Simple Tap

passages.text: That was the architecture decision: the backend has to know what happened, and the phone has to make the action feel light.
headingPath: The Architecture Behind A Simple Tap

passages.text: The diagram zooms out from a snooze tap to the app contract: user action, client app, shared state, access, AI, native surfaces, docs, and distribution stay in their own lanes.
headingPath: The Architecture Behind A Simple Tap

passages.text: AI made sense in Oakminder only if it reduced work.

I did not want the voice feature to become a chatbot panel sitting beside the real app. A reminder app already has a natural input method: say the thing you need to remember. The best version was the one that changed reminder state the user could review.

That choice came from contrast with YouSoul, a different web app I had already built where AI agents communicated and did work through chat. Chat made sense there because the product surface was already an operating room for agents, messages, and task handoffs. Oakminder was different. If the job was remembering something while I was in motion, voice was the shorter bridge between intent and action.
YouSoul was the earlier Kanban and calendar management productivity agent web app where AI agents communicated and did work through chat.

So the voice agent had to do real reminder work. Create a reminder. Edit one. Complete it. Mark it incomplete. Snooze it. Delete it. Create or rename a category. Handle recurring reminder changes. The answer should land inside Oakminder as something the user can review, not as copy the user has to paste somewhere else.

Water Drops (the in-app currency name for AI credits) made that decision more concrete. Voice and agentic features have a visible cost boundary inside the product. That keeps AI usage tied to the business model instead of hiding it as magic. The model work uses Gemini / Vertex AI (https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs) through backend actions, so the voice feature can land as structured reminder state instead of a loose chat response.

Outcome status table Area | Status | Detail | 
 Create | Reminder state | A spoken request becomes a scheduled reminder with title, date, time, and reviewable state. | 
 Manage | Reminder actions | Voice can edit, complete, snooze, delete, and mark reminders incomplete. | 
 Organize | Categories | The same interface can create, rename, or delete categories when the user wants to stay hands-free. | 
 Price boundary | Water Drops | AI usage stays visible through credits that are part of the product model. |
One Oakminder voice-agent scenario: using speech to operate reminder state inside the app.
Building a mobile app also taught me that onboarding is part of the product.

Good mobile onboarding does more than show welcome screens. It explains the product, teaches only what the user needs right now, and moves them into one useful action. For a reminder app, that action is simple: create a reminder, understand why notifications matter, and see how the app will help when the reminder comes back.

Mobile apps ask for trust quickly. Apple onboarding guidance (https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/onboarding) and Android onboarding guidance (https://developer.android.com/design/ui/mobile/guides/patterns/onboarding) both point to the same product lesson: explain the value before asking for commitment. Android’s notification-permission docs make Permission timing even more concrete: ask in context, when the user understands what the notifications are for. That matched what I was learning. Notification permission should not feel like a random system prompt. The app has to explain why it needs that permission, then ask near the moment where the user understands the value. The same is true for AI and voice-agent features in general: explain what the agent can actually do, let the user see the value, then make the subscription boundary feel connected to that value.

I was studying a lot from indie and startup mobile app founders during this period, especially how they handled onboarding and pricing surfaces. I kept seeing the same lesson from different angles: onboarding can hook the user, make monetization feel earned, and help the product sustain usage over a longer period. For Oakminder, that made onboarding part of the product work, not a screen I could leave until the end.
The intro screen frames Oakminder before asking for setup work.
Proof comes early, so the product promise is concrete before permission prompts.
Q&A turns onboarding into a short product conversation, not a static tour.
Visual education screens explain useful reminder facts and tips before asking the user to act.
The comparison frame positions Oakminder against money and time users already spend trying to stay organized.
The permission and paywall step belongs near the end, with trial framing after the product has earned enough trust.

These are featured moments from a much larger onboarding path, not the full flow. Oakminder’s onboarding went closer to 30-40 screens because the product needed to explain reminders, voice, habits, permission timing, and pricing before asking for commitment. One surprising discovery from studying mobile onboarding was that more screens can work when they stay engaging. If each screen teaches something useful, shows the product visually, or helps the user recognize their own problem, the flow can hook people more than a short generic setup.
The docs became part of the product and distribution work.

In the AI and agent age, documentation has a bigger job than support. It helps users understand the product, helps a company keep its own product story consistent, and gives AI tools cleaner context to answer from. If people are going to ask agents how a product works, the product needs a source of truth those agents can read.
Oakminder's documentation page, built with Mintlify.

I tried Mintlify (https://www.mintlify.com/) because I kept seeing AI-related companies use it, and the platform was already leaning into the same things I cared about: Human-readable docs, Markdown pages, llms.txt, MCP, and agent-friendly indexing. For Oakminder, that meant documenting the actual product shape: custom snooze, recurring reminders, cross-device sync, voice actions, native alarms, Live Activity, Agenda Explorer, analytics, categories, support, privacy, terms, and the AI-readable docs surface.

I also started using my coding-agent environment to maintain the docs. When I added or changed a feature, I could ask agents to draft or update the relevant Mintlify pages quickly, then review the result in the same product language as the app. That made documentation feel less like a separate chore and more like part of the build loop: ship the feature, explain it clearly, and keep the explanation friendly to users and AI agents.
Mintlify gives Oakminder docs, llms.txt, and MCP surfaces so AI agents can explore the product with real context.
Putting Oakminder on the App Store answered one question: can I ship the app?
headingPath: After The App Store, Distribution Started

passages.text: The harder question came right after: can I explain it well enough for the market to care?
headingPath: After The App Store, Distribution Started

passages.text: Oakminder on the App Store.
headingPath: After The App Store, Distribution Started

passages.text: That question has become more important because AI agents make software faster to build. A motivated solo builder can create a working app far quicker than before. That is good for builders, and rough on attention. More products can reach the same feeds, app stores, and search results.
headingPath: After The App Store, Distribution Started

passages.text: So the work could not stop at the app. I had to think about distribution: who has the pain, which platform can reach them, which hooks make the product click, which UGC examples feel believable, which onboarding moment earns trust, and which feedback should change the product.
headingPath: After The App Store, Distribution Started

passages.text: The lesson kept coming back: distribution deserves the same taste as the product. A mobile app can grow through ads, organic content, founder-led posts, UGC, partnerships, and a dozen other paths. One channel I liked studying was Superwall (https://www.youtube.com/@SuperwallHQ), because they interview successful startup and indie mobile app founders about paywalls, onboarding, UGC, pricing, and growth loops. The pattern I kept seeing was that product and distribution are often different strengths. TikTok creator tools (https://www.tiktok.com/business/en-US/blog/open-application-campaigns-creator-marketplace) made that obvious: some teams work with real creators who can explain the product in their own voice, while others use GenAI to produce creator-style drafts for their own channels. Either way, the product has to be packaged, explained, tested, and revised with real product context.
headingPath: After The App Store, Distribution Started

passages.text: A channel I kept returning to while learning how founders build and market mobile apps.
headingPath: After The App Store, Distribution Started

passages.text: I also had a gut feeling about where software is moving. As AI agents, local LLMs, and personal automation get better, more people will expect their own small, specific tools instead of only using giant generic platforms. Creators, founders, and small teams can now build closer to the exact problem they have. That is where Personal software started to feel connected to distribution for me.
headingPath: After The App Store, Distribution Started

passages.text: I stopped looking for one perfect growth tool after that. After studying the space, researching TikTok and UGC patterns, and iterating on the product story, I decided to build my own Distribution studio: smaller, more specific, and tied directly to Oakminder’s product context.
headingPath: After The App Store, Distribution Started

passages.text: After shipping the app, I built a separate studio around it.
headingPath: The Distribution Studio Around The App

passages.text: Its job is to help me market the app, learn from TikTok (https://newsroom.tiktok.com/tiktok-world-26-turning-discovery-into-business-growth-with-ai-powered-innovations-vertical-experiences-and-high-impact-brand-solutions) and UGC patterns, create content assets, brief human partners, prepare AI-assisted creator drafts, and route feedback back into product strategy. The target platform was TikTok first because short-form video is where productivity apps can be explained through real-life moments instead of static feature lists.
headingPath: The Distribution Studio Around The App

passages.text: The studio tracks the things a founder needs while trying to make the market understand a product: product positioning, audience, pain points, competitor examples, creator examples, hooks, saved content, traces, transcripts, screenshots, captions, draft slides, video scenes, account context, export state, and feedback.
headingPath: The Distribution Studio Around The App

passages.text: Saved playbooks give me a readable reference library and reusable context for AI agents.
headingPath: The Distribution Studio Around The App

passages.text: The video editor supports quick content production with AI agents, manual edits, inspiration sources, and TikTok slideshow transforms.
headingPath: The Distribution Studio Around The App

passages.text: Global product context and instructions stay available across the app, agentic development work, and AI agents.
headingPath: The Distribution Studio Around The App

passages.text: Related X tips, tricks, and bookmarked posts are saved specifically for Oakminder research.
headingPath: The Distribution Studio Around The App

passages.text:
Outcome status table Area | Status | Detail |

 Research intake | TikTok and UGC signals | Collect competitors, creators, bookmarks, links, saved media, traces, transcripts, comments, frames, and visual patterns. | 
 Context extraction | Trace and OCR | Turn a TikTok URL into metadata, transcript, frame text, visual placement, and traceable context. |

headingPath: The Distribution Studio Around The App

passages.text: The studio stays useful when research, source saving, extraction, draft creation, publishing, and feedback keep product context in the loop.
headingPath: The Distribution Studio Around The App

passages.text: TikTok research happens on phones, but production work happens on larger screens.
headingPath: The Phone Became The Research Bridge

passages.text: That created a practical problem. I might be scrolling TikTok on an Android phone or iPhone and find a creator, competitor, hook, slideshow, comment pattern, or ad style worth saving. If that insight stays on the phone, it becomes a loose note. If it moves into the studio with context, it becomes useful material.
headingPath: The Phone Became The Research Bridge

passages.text: So I built mobile bridge surfaces. From the phone, I can paste a TikTok link, choose the relevant account or context, and send the source into the system. The desktop side can then inspect the trace, use the extracted material, and turn it into a draft or strategy note.
headingPath: The Phone Became The Research Bridge

passages.text: That bridge also fit how I actually work: MacBook and Mac mini for dashboard, editing, rendering, and review; Android and iOS phones for TikTok discovery, mobile review, and source intake.
headingPath: The Phone Became The Research Bridge

passages.text:
01 Notice Find a TikTok pattern, creator, competitor, hook, slideshow, comment angle, or visual style while using a phone.
 02 Send Paste the TikTok URL into the mobile bridge and attach the account or context that makes the source useful.
 03 Extract Bring back creator context, caption or description, comments where supported, transcript, frames, text, and trace IDs.
 04 Produce Use the desktop studio to turn that context into a draft, brief, slideshow, video, or strategy update.
headingPath: The Phone Became The Research Bridge

passages.text: The diagram shows the phone as intake and the desktop as the workspace: TikTok links enter with context, then become organized research traces for drafts and briefs.
headingPath: The Phone Became The Research Bridge

passages.text: For one piece of content, manual notes are enough. At volume, inspiration needs structure.

The trace pipeline is where the distribution studio starts to feel different from a folder of saved links. I wanted each trace to preserve the surroundings of an idea: creator context, caption or description, transcript, music context, frames, screenshots, text in frames, and traceable IDs. For slideshows and videos, the visible text is part of the creative pattern, so I used Google Cloud Vision (https://cloud.google.com/vision/docs/ocr) for text recognition and bounding-box extraction. That gave me the words on the frame plus their placement, space, and layout role.

For content creation, the useful signal is often visual. Where does the hook sit? How much text is on the slide? Which frame sells the idea? What is the rhythm between caption, overlay, image, and CTA? The system does not need to perfectly clone a source. It needs enough context and visual structure to help a human creator, a generated creator-style draft, or an internal edit stay grounded in a real format.

The same Context extraction path feeds the creative side. Once the system has the product angle, source notes, transcript, frame sequence, visual text, and layout cues, it can help build a slideshow draft, rewrite a caption, brief a UGC partner, or give a generative workflow better inputs than “make a productivity ad.” The point is to keep the useful parts of the inspiration alive as it moves through the studio.
Overall post context includes description, caption, interaction numbers, music, and traceable IDs.
AI analysis turns provided details, transcript, and high-level context into strategy material for humans, agents, tools, and team handoff.
Google Cloud Vision and specialized algorithms extract text recognition plus bounding boxes, size, font, and text style for easier volume content creation and repurposing.
Deeper frame-by-frame visual analysis gives AI agents and systems more useful slide context.
Once research becomes structured context, the next question is production.

The studio needed a place where product angle, source notes, and extracted inspiration could turn into an editable asset. The slideshow editor became the main surface for that. It supports drafts, templates, post mode, inspiration mode, autosave, recovery, slide reorder, generated content, text overlays, image history, per-slide image generation, selected account context, sounds, speed, aspect ratio, CTA presets, content ideas, trace-agent context, caption rewrite, export state, and detail-sheet metadata.

That sounds heavy because the work is heavy. A draft that cannot be edited, reviewed, and traced back to a product angle is just a generated asset. I wanted the draft to keep its memory: why it exists, which product angle it uses, where the source format came from, which account or creator style it belongs to, which visual pattern it borrowed, and how it should leave the editor.

The studio widened from there. Remotion (https://www.remotion.dev/) gave video scenes a rendering path. The hook factory separated hook discovery and CTA production from final slideshow editing. Asset workflows kept local images, generated images, CTA clips, sounds, and replacement media available. Mobile queues made review possible away from the desktop.

Outcome status table Area | Status | Detail | 
 Slideshow editor | Main draft surface | Generate, rearrange, refine, rewrite, replace images, keep source text, save templates, and prepare exports. | 
 Video editor | Rendering lane | Use Remotion-backed scene editing for media, timing, transitions, crop modes, text overlays, preview, drafts, and export. | 
 Hook factory | Batch ideation | Track source channels, extract hooks, store CTA assets, add overlays, choose transitions, and review production runs. | 
 Asset workflows | Material pool | Use local assets, generated images, image history, source library media, CTA clips, sounds, and replacement flows. | 
 Mobile review | Away from desk | Use mobile queue, trace intake, profile display, comment generation, retry, copy, and done-state workflows. |
The slideshow carousel editor brings quick shortcuts, production tools, and AI features into one draft surface.
Campaign asset management makes reuse and templating easier across content runs.
The distribution studio had to support more than one way to produce content.

Some app teams work with real UGC creators. That means the founder needs UGC briefs, examples, product context, do and do-not guidance, hooks, source patterns, tone, and review notes. A creator should not have to guess what the product does or why the user cares.

Other founders use GenAI creator drafts for their own channels. That path still needs context. A generative workflow is much stronger when it has the product angle, target audience, source format, transcript, frame structure, caption direction, CTA, and visual notes.

I built the studio so the same inputs could serve both modes. The system can collect inspiration, extract context, preserve the product angle, and turn the result into a brief, a slideshow draft, a caption rewrite, or an AI-generation input.
Management flows handle the handoff between AI agents, UGC creators, and TikTok account operations.

I also created dedicated OpenClaw agents (https://openclaw.ai/) for specific accounts and niches. Their job is to keep the extracted insights from source material, remember what fit that niche, and improve the next brief or draft with better context. Instead of every creator draft starting from a blank prompt, the account or niche can carry its own memory: product angle, audience, visual taste, hooks, objections, and examples worth reusing.
OpenClaw agents stay organized around the AI accounts and UGC creators they support.
Creative work is incomplete until it can leave the editor and teach the next decision.

So the studio included export health, review states, retry paths, and publishing handoff. I used Postiz (https://postiz.com/) for content scheduling and analytics through its API, but that is only one path. Other content scheduling APIs, social publishing tools, and platform-specific publishing surfaces could fit the same handoff shape later. Browser control is another option when an API path is not the right fit, especially for manual upload, review, or account-specific publishing flows.
The studio works when source context and production action stay connected across research, extraction, drafts, export, and feedback.
The loop works when source context keeps feeding the studio actions that move a draft toward publishing and back into feedback.

The handoff had to account for slideshow exports, draft publishing, retry paths, re-export controls, export health, and review state. For readers, the loop is simple enough: draft, review, handoff, retry, and feedback.

The value is the next turn: product context shapes strategy, TikTok research creates inspiration, extraction creates structured inputs, the studio creates drafts, export moves them toward the platform, and feedback loop updates the next strategy.
Final post details and processing states are checked before scheduling to the target platform.
The part I would keep is the pairing.

Saturated markets still leave room for a product when the lived friction is real. I did not build Oakminder because reminder apps were useless. I built it because the interruption moment felt underserved: too many taps, too much configuration, too little help when attention is already thin.

App builders also need distribution taste alongside product taste. Shipping the app is one kind of signal. Explaining it, testing hooks, briefing creators, and feeding market feedback back into the product is a different kind of work.

AI helped most when it moved work forward. In the app, voice turns natural language into reminder actions. In the distribution studio, agents and extraction workflows turn messy research into drafts, briefs, and feedback. In development, agentic coding helped me move faster, but the product judgment still came from taste, lived use, and the constraints I wrote down for the agents.
The real carryover is the learning and experience behind the systems: the app, distribution studio, and agent workflows gave me reusable pieces for future projects and solutions.

The project also gave me reusable knowledge and experience beyond Oakminder. I am already carrying the app and distribution studio lessons into current and upcoming work: agentic development, mobile onboarding, notification behavior, founder mindset, distribution strategy, UGC workflows, source extraction, creative production systems, AI-assisted content production, and the operating habits around building with agents. Some founders have already reached out about distribution systems and similar agentic production work for content creation niches. I will share more as the system becomes cleaner, and parts of the studio may become open source once the reusable patterns can stand on their own.
That is the version I would build again: one app that solves a specific moment, and one studio that keeps learning how to explain it.

passages.text: The ones who stand out in 2026 accepted a different reality. AI is leverage, not a magic pill.

passages.text: January 30, 2026
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Steve Oak (Okkar Kyaw)
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: AI is incredible. Transformers and attention mechanisms changed the world in a few years. We can automate almost everything now. But here's what nobody talks about enough: the moment you push past the context window, everything falls apart.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: There are solutions out there. Improvements. Workarounds. None of them are permanent fixes.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: The pains we all face? Memory and hallucination. Working with LLMs feels like managing a kid with ADHD sometimes. They completely forget halfway through what they were doing. No memory. And when there's no memory, hallucination follows. You can do compaction, sure. Doesn't help much.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: So how do we actually solve it? Memory. Okay, but how? Markdown. JSON. Indexing. RAG. GRAPH.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Confused? Good. Let me walk you through how a small ML project taught me more about fixing AI's fundamental problems than any tutorial ever could.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Job search.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Layoffs happening for senior talent. Market's brutal for juniors. New AI roles popping up everywhere. Lots of job platforms appearing. The problem? None of them are tailored to you.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: LinkedIn's Job Search AI is limited. ChatGPT and general LLMs are worse. All these new job platforms? Same limitations.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Not because they can't do better. It just makes more sense for them to provide a general experience for everyone. AI features cost a lot of resources. So here's the reality: no company will ever provide actually tailored suggestions for you individually. It's not their fault. They have competition, demands, and they can't prioritize your specific needs.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Don't blame them. Blame yourself.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: With all these powerful tools available now, why not build something tailored for your own needs?
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: That thought stuck with me. I decided to build a mini project that could provide actual tailored suggestions based on user profile, resume documents, job descriptions, company info, real match scores. Everything that matters.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: My approach: verify before showing anything to users. Simple idea, but different from everyone else.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Most AI assistants generate first, check later (or never). SOKK flips this. Every suggestion passes through two verification gates before you see it.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: The Neural Gate uses LLM-as-Judge to verify every claim. If SOKK suggests "Add your GraphQL experience", it checks: Does the job actually require GraphQL? Do you actually have GraphQL experience somewhere in your documents?
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: The Symbolic Gate enforces quality stuff: mentions the job title, cites a real requirement, stays under character limits, professional tone, has a call to action.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: This approach costs more. Gemini for AI, Voyage AI for RAG, Exa for research and crawling, other APIs. Companies building "done-for-you" solutions need to heavily optimize or cut features to operate profitably.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: But for you personally? Spending a few dollars for actually accurate, personalized results makes sense. That's why DIY workflow systems with AI are worth exploring. Open source LLMs make it cheaper now. You have options.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: After SOKK, something clicked. Wait. I can RAG my entire codebase for smarter AI agent development.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: If you use Cursor, GitHub Copilot, or WARP, it's the same thing they call "indexing codebase." Makes the whole experience smarter instead of searching everything every time you ask a question.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: What you get: finding code by meaning instead of just keywords. Only relevant code pulled into context. AI actually understands your patterns, your architecture, how you do things.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: This isn't about finding files faster. It's about giving AI actual understanding of your project instead of treating every question like a fresh start with amnesia.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: I experimented a lot and built my own system called UOCE (Universal Oak Context Engine). It RAGs with two embedding types: Voyage Context for markdown and docs, Voyage Code for actual code. Then reranks everything using RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion).
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Made the system git and commit aware too. It knows what changed recently, what's been stable, what's new.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Three queries run in parallel. OakSearch does hybrid BM25 + Vector search with 0.3/0.7 weighting for the codebase. Serena handles session-specific memory for the current project. CORE is long-term graph memory across all projects.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: But here's the thing. This is stuff everyone does now. It makes AI smarter across the project codebase. Still doesn't solve the context window memory degrading problem though.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: So I fixed the memory problem with a dual-memory architecture.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Serena Memory handles short-term, project-specific context. Saves session context and directory structure. I write handoff notes before every session or when moving to the next task, then load those contexts back for new sessions. Think of it as "where was I" memory spanning hours to weeks.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Graph Memory connects everything like a neural network for long-term storage across all projects. I built my own local Neo4j graph system with Gemini Flash intent search. It saves my preferences, best practices I've learned, architectural decisions. A second brain that gets smarter over time.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: The routing is simple. Session context and implementation notes stay in Serena (temporary, project-specific). Architectural decisions and patterns get promoted to CORE (permanent, cross-project). Temporary debugging notes get deleted.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Here's what took me a while to learn: not everything deserves to be remembered. Smart forgetting matters as much as smart remembering.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: I still had to manually trigger saves and loads. Annoying. So I used Claude hooks to set up smart auto-triggers.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: The hooks use Gemini Flash to identify intent instead of spamming saves on every action. It figures out when something's worth remembering versus when it's just routine debugging noise.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: What the triggers check: Is this a decision or just an experiment? Is this pattern reusable or project-specific? Is this a checkpoint moment or mid-task noise?
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Took the manual overhead out of the memory system. Now it runs in the background, capturing what matters.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Some tools that have worked for me:
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Serena MCP for memory saving and session context. Neo4j or Core Memory for graph storage (Core Memory sets up everything, it's open source. I forked my own version). Morphllm Edit Tool for bulk edits across multiple files. Morphllm Warpgrep Tool for semantic search across the codebase.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: These have helped me get more out of the LLMs I use. The workflow's been good.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Looking back, a few things would have saved me time.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Like I mentioned from Ecosmartloop case study, Context engineering matters more than prompt engineering. Once I started giving AI specific context instead of generic prompts, suggestion quality changed completely. I spent too long trying to write perfect prompts when the problem was always the context.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Build incrementally. I over-engineered the memory system before validating that basic RAG even worked for my use case. Should have proven value at each layer before adding complexity.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Test memory systems early. The handoff protocol was an afterthought. Should have been designed from day one. The amount of context I lost between sessions in the early weeks hurt.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: More aggressive checkpoints. I now save every 30 minutes, not just at session end. Losing an hour of context to a crash taught me that one the hard way.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: This isn't just for coding. You can see the same patterns showing up in general chat products now.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: Perplexity, GPT, Grok are all adding memory across chats. The industry figured out that stateless AI conversations hit a ceiling. Memory's becoming expected.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

passages.text: The patterns I built for SOKK and UOCE are the same patterns these companies are implementing at scale. I just built mine tailored for my specific workflow.
headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination

headingPath: How a Small ML Project Accidentally Helped Me Solve AI's Biggest Problems: Memory & Hallucination
